title: A reusable pipeline
story:
The artefact you ship is not a model. It is a route from raw input to prediction, and every step along that route which learned anything from data is part of the model whether or not it is stored with one.

That is the argument for making the whole route a single fitted object rather than a sequence of steps in a notebook. The documentation puts the leakage case directly: the pipeline prevents leakage because it ensures the appropriate method is performed on the correct data subset, and it is ideal for cross-validation and hyper-parameter tuning — which is exactly where a hand-rolled sequence goes wrong, because preprocessing done before the loop is done once on everything, and the folds inside the loop then score against rows that have already influenced the transformation.

The second failure is at the other end and is even less forgiving. If these transforms are used when training a model, they must also be used on subsequent datasets, whether test data or data in a production system, because otherwise the feature space will change and the model will not be able to perform effectively. The documented illustration is stark: a mean squared error of 62.80 when the transform is skipped at prediction time against 0.90 when it is applied. Same model, same weights, same input data. The entire difference is one step that lived in the training script and not in the serving path — and the score it produces is bad rather than absent, so nothing tells you except the metric.

Reproducibility is the third leg and the guidance on it is specific. For results that are constant across executions you must remove every use of an unset random state; the recommended approach is to declare one generator at the top of the program and pass it into every object that accepts one, and explicitly not to set the array library's global seed instead. The distinction matters because an unset default draws from global entropy, so two runs of the same script on the same data give two different artefacts, and you cannot tell whether a change you made improved anything or whether you reran it.

Finally, the thing that makes all of this harder than it sounds. Sculley and colleagues describe models as machines for creating entanglement, which makes isolating improvements effectively impossible: changing the input distribution of one feature may alter the importance, weights or use of all the remaining features, and adding or removing a feature does the same, because no inputs are ever really independent. They call it the CACE principle — Changing Anything Changes Everything — and note that it applies not only to input signals but to hyper-parameters, learning settings, sampling methods, convergence thresholds and data selection. That is why the unit of evaluation has to be the whole route. You cannot improve one step and reason locally about the consequences, so the pipeline is not only how you prevent leakage; it is the only thing whose behaviour you can actually measure.

problem.name: The fitted pipeline
aka: preprocessing as part of the model
problem.shape: A prediction requires several steps applied in order, some of which learned their parameters from data, and the whole sequence has to run identically at training time and at serving time.
tell: preprocessing happens in one script and prediction in another
a transformation is fitted before the cross-validation loop
rerunning the same code on the same data gives a different model
a step was improved in isolation and the overall result moved unpredictably
problem.move: Make the entire route one fitted object, so that the boundary between learning and applying is structural rather than remembered, and pass that object to cross-validation and tuning so preprocessing is refitted inside every fold. Declare a single random generator at the top of the program and pass it to everything that takes one. Evaluate end to end, and change one thing at a time so attribution stays clean.
problem.invariant: Every step that learned from data is part of the model. It must be fitted only on training data, and it must accompany the model everywhere the model goes, or the inputs at serving time are not the inputs it was fitted for.
problem.breaks: Packaging the route correctly does not make its parts independently improvable. The parameters were fitted jointly, so changing one step's output distribution changes the importance and weights of every other feature — which means the pipeline gives you something you can measure and still not something you can reason about a piece at a time.

cost.time: refitting preprocessing inside every fold rather than once, which multiplies the preprocessing cost by the number of folds and is almost always worth it
cost.space: the fitted transformers ship with the model, so the artefact is larger than the weights alone — which is the point
cost.beats: keeping preprocessing in a separate script, which is faster to write, leaks into cross-validation at one end, and diverges from the serving path at the other

worked.problem: You improved one feature's preprocessing in isolation and overall accuracy fell. How is that possible?
worked.reasoning:
Because the steps are not independent, and a model is a machine for making them dependent on each other.

The intuition being violated is the one that works everywhere else in software. Normally a component has an interface, you improve what is behind the interface, and the callers are unaffected. A fitted model has no such boundary. Its parameters were chosen jointly, against the distribution of all the features simultaneously, so the weights on every other feature are partly a function of what this one was doing.

Change one feature's preprocessing — scale it differently, impute it differently, clip its outliers — and you have changed its input distribution. On the next fit, the importance, weights and use of the remaining features change too, because the optimiser is solving a different joint problem. A feature that was carrying some of this one's signal may now be down-weighted; a redundancy that was providing robustness may vanish. Nothing about the other steps' code changed, and their contribution did.

This is the CACE principle: Changing Anything Changes Everything. And it is broader than features — it applies to hyper-parameters, learning settings, sampling methods, convergence thresholds and data selection, all of which are entangled in the same way. No inputs are ever really independent.

There are also two more ordinary explanations to rule out first, because they are more common than the interesting one. The improvement may have been fitted on more data than it should have been, in which case the old score was honest and the new one is inflated or the comparison is not like for like. And the change may have made training and serving disagree, where the transform improved but only in one of the two paths, which shows up as a bad score rather than an error.

Practically, this is why the whole route has to be one object and the unit of evaluation has to be the entire pipeline. Component-level reasoning is not available here. You evaluate end to end, you hold everything else fixed and change one thing at a time so that the attribution is at least clean, and you accept that a local improvement is a hypothesis about the system rather than a property of the step. The mitigation the authors suggest is to detect changes in prediction behaviour as they occur, through continuous monitoring, rather than expecting to reason your way to the effect in advance.

problem.practice: Take a model you have built across several scripts and rebuild it as a single fitted object, then confirm that cross-validation scores change once preprocessing is refitted inside each fold. Then run the whole thing twice from a cold start and check that you get a byte-identical artefact — if you do not, find the unset random state.

beats.broke: What gets shipped is not a model but a route from raw input to prediction, and every step on that route which learned anything from data is part of the model and has to travel with it.
beats.fix: Make the whole route one fitted object, so the boundary between learning and applying is structural rather than remembered, and so the same code runs at training time and at serving time.
beats.cost: The components stop being independently testable: because the parameters were fitted jointly, changing any one step changes the weights and use of all the others, so the unit of evaluation becomes the whole route rather than any part of it.

interview.q: You improved one feature's preprocessing in isolation and overall accuracy fell. How is that possible?
interview.trap: Assuming a bug, or that the improvement was not really an improvement. The step may well be better in isolation; a fitted model has no component boundary, so a better input distribution for one feature is a different joint problem for all of them.
interview.answer:
Because the steps are not independent, and a fitted model is a machine for making them depend on each other.

The intuition being violated is the one that holds everywhere else in software: a component has an interface, you improve what sits behind it, and callers are unaffected. A fitted model has no such boundary. Its parameters were chosen jointly against the distribution of all the features at once, so the weight on every other feature is partly a function of what this one was doing.

Change one feature's preprocessing — a different scaling, a different imputation, clipped outliers — and you have changed its input distribution. On the next fit, the importance, weights and use of the remaining features change too, because the optimiser is now solving a different joint problem. A feature that had been carrying some of this one's signal may get down-weighted; a redundancy that was providing robustness may disappear. No other step's code changed, and every other step's contribution did. That is the CACE principle — Changing Anything Changes Everything — and it extends beyond features to hyper-parameters, learning settings, sampling methods, convergence thresholds and data selection, because no inputs are ever really independent.

I would rule out two duller explanations first, since they are more common. The improved step may have been fitted on more data than it should have been, making the comparison unlike for like. And the change may have made training and serving disagree, improving the transform in one path only — which surfaces as a poor score rather than an error.

What follows practically is that component-level reasoning is not available here. The unit of evaluation is the whole route, which is the deeper reason to make it a single fitted object. I change one thing at a time for clean attribution rather than for local reasoning, treat a local improvement as a hypothesis about the system until measured end to end, and rely on monitoring prediction behaviour as it changes rather than expecting to reason out the effect in advance.

   raw input

   inside the artefact -> no train/serve skew

   remove every unset random state
   ONE generator, declared at the top,
   passed down
   NOT the global seed of the array library

   otherwise: two runs, two artefacts, and no
   way to tell a real improvement from a rerun

takeaway: Every step that learned from data is part of the model and must be fitted inside the fold and shipped with the weights — and because the parameters were fitted jointly, the assembled route is the only thing you can measure, never a piece of it.
